summary_paragraph: A 60-year-old male with a history of kidney transplantation, type 2 diabetes, hypertension, and coronary artery disease was admitted for severe bilateral knee pain, initially suspected to be septic arthritis or cellulitis. The patient had persistent right knee pain despite outpatient antibiotics, with subsequent left knee involvement. Workup revealed a markedly elevated uric acid level of 12.3 mg/dL, elevated inflammatory markers, and imaging showing bilateral knee effusions without evidence of infection or crystals. Lyme serology was negative. Given the high clinical suspicion for gout and improvement with steroids, he was treated with a prednisone taper and started on allopurinol. Acute kidney injury, likely pre-renal from poor intake and diuretic use, improved with IV fluids. Tacrolimus was increased due to subtherapeutic levels, and hydrochlorothiazide was discontinued to reduce gout risk. Blood pressure and glucose were managed with medication adjustments. The patient improved clinically and was discharged home with a plan for outpatient follow-up in rheumatology, nephrology, and primary care.
problems: Hypertensive chronic kidney disease with stage 1 through stage 4 chronic kidney disease, or unspecified chronic kidney disease
